nodes.body: The platform clock had stopped at twelve minutes past eleven, though it was nearer midnight now, and the station lamps burned orange through the first wet flakes of snow. {~HERO:Vera~} crossed the platform with her bag low in her hand, the sleet turning soft and silent against her coat as the temperature dropped. The last northbound overnight train of the season stood open on the track, breathing steam into the dark like an animal that had been waiting a very long time. Its windows threw long yellow panels across the platform, and inside them figures moved with the deliberate, unhurried calm of passengers who had been aboard since before the timetable began. A conductor with a silver punch-clock stood at the open door of the third carriage, watching {~HERO:Vera~} approach without speaking, his face pale and still as a photograph. She stepped up, and the carriage received her with a shiver of heat and old wool.

choices.label: Find a seat and take it in.

nodes.body: The carriage was nearly empty and somehow full at once: a scatter of travellers in the amber light, each bent toward a private stillness. The windows gave back only the interior—reflections layered over the dark country beyond, Vera’s own face a pale ghost over fields she could not see. The air smelled of coffee and cold metal and something older, an attic smell, the breath of a room closed for the season. Four ways forward opened around her. The night conductor hadn’t moved from his post. Low curtains stirred in the sleeper corridor. Something pale lay folded on the seat across the aisle, and outside the cold glass the snow was beginning to stick.

{~HERO:Vera~} walked toward him between the rows of empty seats. The carriage swayed under her with the long, slow rhythm of a line laid down decades before anyone aboard was born. The night conductor stood at the carriage end. His silver punch-clock was in one hand, and the other rested on the door frame. He was a man who had stood in this exact way on this exact train for longer than made sense. The cold glass beside him held her reflection over the dark—her own tired face, the smudge of her collar, the way the shadows cut her in half at the window. Behind her reflection, snow was falling into a country she did not recognise. He looked at her and did not look at her, both at once. The dial of his punch-clock showed a time that matched no station they had passed.

The punch-clock was silver and old, heavy enough to leave a mark if it fell, and the conductor held it with the casual ownership of a man who had never set it down. {~HERO:Vera~} could see the card inside, a pale rectangle of stiff paper with names stamped in faded ink—stations, maybe, or passengers—and the hands of the small face above the card stood at four-seventeen, a time that had no business on a midnight train. Two ways to read this opened before her. She could step right up and ask him what the clock was keeping, point-blank, and risk shutting the whole thing down. Or she could stay in the shadow of the luggage rack and let the rhythm of the carriage teach her what he wouldn’t say.

“That clock,” {~HERO:Vera~} said, and the conductor looked at her fully for the first time, his eyes a pale grey that seemed to have no pupil in the low light. “It’s wrong.” He turned the punch-clock over in his hands, and she saw that the card wasn’t a card at all but a strip of names, dozens of them, stamped in a column that ran off the bottom edge into the brass casing, and every name was followed by a date she didn’t recognise. “It keeps what it keeps,” he said, and tucked it back against his chest. The fact lodged in her mind like a splinter: the card went on, and on, and the names weren’t passengers—they were years.

From the half-shadow of the luggage rack {~HERO:Vera~} watched the conductor work the card from the punch-clock with two fingers, glance at it, and feed it back in with a small brass lever she had not seen before. The motion was rehearsed, intimate, the gesture of a man who had done this ten thousand times and would do it ten thousand more. The carriage rocked gently, and the warmth of the heating pipes was pulling at her eyelids, turning the scene at the end of the aisle into something she could watch without quite being in. The fact was there, soft and stubborn: the man was not keeping time for this train. He was keeping it for the line itself, for every train that had ever run it, and the clock was older than he was. She could carry the thread forward while it was still sharp, or she could let the dark and the motion close over her and see what was left in the morning.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: Something about the conductor’s clock had slipped sideways in the telling. {~HERO:Vera~} turned the fact over as she walked: it wasn’t only that the card held names, or that the hands had stopped at a dead hour. It was that the conductor had never looked at his own face in the window glass beside her, not once, as though he knew there was nothing there to see. The carriage seemed to tighten around the wrongness, drawing it into the walls, the seats, the slow sway of the couplings. Even the heating pipes had quietened. The journey had caught its breath and was waiting for her to notice.

The wrongness had a shape now, and {~HERO:Vera~} carried it with her through the next two cars like a stone in her pocket. She passed a carriage where four people sat in the dining nook with empty cups in front of them. She passed another where a child was awake and watching the aisle with patient, unsurprised eyes. The whole train seemed to be breathing around a single heavy centre, a question it had been carrying since long before she got on. The couplings gave their low iron sigh. {~HERO:Vera~}’s reflection was still there in the glass, still walking, and the country beyond it was black and unreeling.

The warmth of the carriage was a slow tide and {~HERO:Vera~} did not feel it take her. One moment the conductor was still there at the end of the aisle, his silver clock half-turned toward her, and the next the light had shifted and the seat beside her was cold and the carriage had emptied of everything but the sound of the rails. She surfaced dry-mouthed and disoriented, the card, the names, the look he hadn’t given the glass—all of it gone, slid back under the surface of the night before she could close her hand around it. The train was still moving north. She was safe. But the bright edge of the thing she had almost grasped had passed, and she sat in the quiet carriage knowing she had missed her moment, and the journey would not offer it again.

The sleeper corridor was narrower than the main carriages, a long creaking passage lined with heavy green curtains drawn across every berth. {~HERO:Vera~} walked slowly, the carriage swaying under her and the window glass on her left throwing back a duplicate of the corridor—her own face moving through it, pale and unmoored, a woman walking inside the dark. The air was close and breathed-in, warm wool and old lavender and the faint iron smell of the heating pipes. Behind the curtains nothing stirred, no cough, no rustle of a turning body, and yet the berths felt occupied in the particular way a room feels occupied when someone has just left it. A small detail caught at her attention: one curtain, halfway down, was tied open with a piece of red string.

The berth behind the tied curtain was empty, but the pillow held the clear impression of a head, and a book lay open on the blanket with its spine up, pages splayed. {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the narrow corridor with the carriage rocking under her, deciding how to read the room. Two ways opened. She could sweep the curtain aside and search the berth properly, looking for what the passenger had been reading, what they had left, risking the sudden return of whoever had lain there. Or she could stay in the corridor and let the long row of curtained berths tell her their story in their own time—the red string, the open book, the head-shaped hollow in the pillow—while the train kept whatever secrets it held.

{~HERO:Vera~} stepped into the berth and picked up the book. It was a timetable—not the glossy fold-out kind but a hand-bound volume of thin paper, columns of stations and times inked in a script so small it seemed to have been written with a needle. The pages went on past any reasonable route, past the northernmost stations she had ever heard of, and the ink on the later pages was a different colour, a faded brown that looked like very old blood. The fact landed with a small cold shock: this wasn’t a passenger’s timetable. This was the train’s own memory of every stop it had ever made, and someone was still writing it.

From the corridor {~HERO:Vera~} could see the book without touching it, and she noticed something she might have missed if she’d gone in: the red string wasn’t holding the curtain open. It was tied to the curtain ring and looped across the berth to the far wall, where it disappeared under the mattress, pulled taut. A line. Someone was marking a path through the sleeper car. The observation was small but it changed the shape of the corridor behind her: all those closed green curtains, and a thread running through them. She could follow it forward into whatever it was mapping, or she could let the hour and the warmth of the heating pipes pull her down before she had to decide.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The berth and the corridor had delivered the same small ache, different only in the angle of approach: the sleeper car was not a place of rest. It was a place of record. Every berth held the trace of someone who had lain down knowing something, and the book and the red string were two ways of saying the same thing—someone was keeping track, and the track ran deeper than the rails. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the journey draw tight around her, the way a held breath tightens a chest. Even the carriage seemed quieter now, the wheels on the iron a softer, more patient sound.

The sleeper car had handed {~HERO:Vera~} a thread and she followed it forward, through the next coupling, past the dining car where the lights were still on and no one was eating. The question at the heart of the train felt closer now, a hum under the floorboards, a pulse in the iron. What were they all riding toward? Not a station—no station could hold what the timetable described, what the red string was measuring, what the conductor’s clock was adding up. Something else was pulling them north, and the train was built around it the way a cathedral is built around an altar.

The warmth in the sleeper corridor was a hand on {~HERO:Vera~}’s shoulder, pressing down. She meant to follow the red string to the next berth, meant to hold the image of the open book and its impossible columns, but the sway of the carriage was a cradle and the night was deep and the fact she had almost caught dissolved before she could name it. She woke later in a different carriage, the sleeper cars far behind her, the string, the book, the head-shaped hollow in the pillow all receding into a story she had nearly read. The train was still moving. She was unhurt. But she had been offered a door and she had let it close, and the journey ahead felt thinner for it.

ending.title: A Door You Did Not Open

nodes.body: The letter lay folded on the seat across the aisle, a pale rectangle on dark upholstery, no envelope, no address. {~HERO:Vera~} picked it up and the paper was cold in her fingers, colder than the carriage air, as though it had been carried a long way through the snow before being set down here. The carriage swayed and the window glass held her reflection over the moving dark, her own face bent toward the page, a woman reading in a half-lit train. The hand was small and neat, a stranger’s hand, the ink blue-black and slightly smudged at the edges. It began without a greeting. The first line read: I am sitting two carriages ahead of you, and I will be gone before the tunnel.

The letter was written on both sides of a single sheet, and the hand grew shakier near the end as though the writer had been running out of time or nerve. {~HERO:Vera~} held it under the reading lamp and watched the words swim in and out of the warm yellow pool. Two ways to read it opened before her. She could turn the page over and take in the whole thing at once—the warning, the confession, whatever name was signed at the bottom—and risk having the stranger in the forward carriage know she had read it. Or she could fold the letter, set it back on the seat, and watch the aisle for movement, letting the words she had already read work on her slowly while the train kept its larger silence.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned the page. The second side was shorter and the handwriting had begun to break apart, the letters loosening into a scrawl that was harder to read. The writer said they had been on the train for six nights and could no longer remember the station where they boarded, that the conductor’s clock had shown their name before they gave it, and that the mountain tunnel was closer than the timetable claimed. There was no signature. Only a date at the bottom, written clearly, and the date was four years old. The fact sat in {~HERO:Vera~}’s mind like a stone dropped into still water: the paper was fresh, the ink recent, and the date was impossible.

{~HERO:Vera~} folded the letter and set it back on the seat, watching the aisle over its pale edge. For a long moment nothing moved, and then a woman in grey rose from a seat two carriages ahead—{~HERO:Vera~} could just see her through the connecting doors—and walked toward the vestibule without looking back. The letter’s first line rang in {~HERO:Vera~}’s head: I am sitting two carriages ahead of you, and I will be gone before the tunnel. The woman had not been wearing grey when she sat down. Or had she? The observation was soft at the edges, but it carried a weight she couldn’t shake. She could hold this thread and follow it forward, or she could let the hour and the motion ease her under before the choice hardened.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The letter had seeded something in {~HERO:Vera~} that grew in the dark. It wasn’t only the impossible date or the woman in grey; it was the way the handwriting had broken open near the end, as if the writer had been trying to get the words down before the tunnel took their nerve. The letter was a message passed forward through the train, and {~HERO:Vera~} had caught it, and now the message was inside her. The carriage felt narrower than it had, the air closer, the wheels on the iron a slower and more deliberate rhythm, as though the train itself were waiting to see what she would do with what she carried.

The letter had given {~HERO:Vera~} a question she could not put down: who writes a warning on a train that never arrives, and dates it four years ago, and leaves it on a seat for a stranger to find? She walked forward through the swaying cars and the question walked with her, a quiet companion, a second heartbeat. The train seemed to be built around it—the conductor’s impossible clock, the sleeper berths full of absent sleepers, the child who watched the aisle with eyes that had seen more than a child’s eyes should see. All of it led toward a centre, a heavy stillness at the heart of the night, and {~HERO:Vera~} was being pulled toward it.

The words on the page began to blur. {~HERO:Vera~} tried to hold the date, the handwriting, the woman in grey, but the warmth of the carriage was pulling her down and the letter grew soft in her hands, the ink running into the paper like water into sand. She surfaced later with the sheet still folded on her lap and the carriage empty around her, the stranger’s warning gone, the details dissolved into a vague unease she couldn’t pin to anything real. The train was still moving. She was safe. But the letter had said something important, something she had nearly understood, and now it was only a sheet of cold paper with no voice left in it.

{~HERO:Vera~} pressed her forehead to the cold glass and watched the black country slide past the window, a landscape without landmarks, fields and cuttings and the occasional dark stand of trees that might have been pines. The carriage swayed and the window held her reflection over the dark, her own tired face floating above the snow that was beginning to stick to the ledges. For a long time there was nothing but the rhythm of the wheels and the small white flakes spinning out of the dark, and then something changed. A station went by—no platform, no name-board, only a single lamp burning on a post—and the lamp was lit, and the station was clearly abandoned. A first detail pulled at her attention: the lamp had been lit recently enough that the glass was still free of snow.

The black country sliding past the window was not as empty as it had first seemed. {~HERO:Vera~} watched, and after a while another station went by—a bare wooden shelter, a bench, a name-board she couldn’t read in the dark—and this one had two lamps burning, and a figure standing under the shelter with its back to the train. Two ways to read the landscape opened before her. She could keep her face to the glass and hunt for the next station, the next light, the next impossible figure, pressing the dark for a pattern it didn’t want to give. Or she could sit back and let the country come to her in its own time, the lit lamps and the standing figures and the stations that weren’t on any map, while the train kept its secret and the snow fell.

{~HERO:Vera~} kept her face to the glass and counted. In the next twenty minutes the train passed six stations, and every one was lit, and every one was empty of anyone but a single figure standing with its back to the rails. The stations were not on the line. They couldn’t be—they came too fast, too close together, the lamps a warm amber that didn’t belong to any railway company she knew. The fact came to her not as a thought but as a physical sensation, a cold settling into her stomach: the landscape outside was not the landscape the train was travelling through. The journey was happening on two tracks, and one of them was not on any map.

{~HERO:Vera~} sat back from the glass and let the country unspool at the edge of her vision, not chasing it, not counting. The lit stations came anyway, slow and steady, lamps burning in the snow, figures standing in the shelters, and after a while she noticed something she might have missed if she’d been hunting for it: the figures were the same figure. The same stoop of the shoulders, the same dark coat, the same way of standing with the hands in the pockets. The country outside was repeating itself, a loop of stations and snow and the one patient figure waiting for a train that had already passed. The observation was soft, not hard enough to hold, but it was there. She could carry it forward into the night, or she could let the warmth of the carriage close over her before she had to make sense of it.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The stations outside and the train inside had converged on the same quiet disorder. The country was not a country; it was a passage, a stretch of dark the train had been crossing for longer than any timetable could measure, and the lit platforms were markers of something—arrivals, departures, moments when a journey stopped being a journey and became a destination. {~HERO:Vera~} felt the train close around her like a held breath, the walls pressing in, the carriage air gone still. The wheels on the iron were slower now, or she was hearing them differently, a long patient rhythm that had been going on since before she was born.

The dark country had given {~HERO:Vera~} a key, and she carried it with her through the next two cars, past the dining nook where four passengers still sat with empty cups, past the sleeper corridor with its drawn green curtains and its red string. The train was not travelling north. It was travelling inward, toward a centre that was also a threshold, and every passenger aboard was riding toward the same still point. The question the whole train was built around had a shape now, and the shape was the tunnel ahead, and the dawn beyond it.

The rhythm of the wheels was a lullaby and {~HERO:Vera~} didn’t feel it take her. One moment the black country was sliding past the window with its impossible lit stations and its single patient figure, and the next the light in the carriage had shifted and the glass was grey with the first suggestion of morning. She surfaced slowly, her neck stiff, her mind empty of the country she had been reading. The stations, the lamps, the figure under the shelter—all of it had gone, slipped back behind the surface of the night before she could name what it meant. The train was still moving, safe and warm and indifferent, and she sat in the half-light knowing she had been shown something and had let it go.

The dining car was lit with small amber lamps set into the walls, and at a table near the window four passengers sat with empty cups before them and nothing on the plates. {~HERO:Vera~} walked toward them and the carriage swayed, carrying her reflection across the dark glass, a woman moving through a room where no one was eating. The passengers did not look up. They were seated in the postures of people who had been there a long time—one man with his coat still on, a woman with her gloves folded beside her spoon, two others whose faces were turned toward the window as though the black country outside were a programme they were following. A detail caught at {~HERO:Vera~}: none of them had ordered anything, but the cups were full of something that steamed gently, and the steam had no smell.

The dining car had the settled, inhabited quiet of a room that had been occupied for years. {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the aisle and the four passengers did not turn toward her, did not acknowledge her presence, and yet she felt herself being read—the weight of her coat, the weariness in her face, the question she was carrying. Two ways to approach them opened. She could sit down at the table, introduce herself, ask them directly why they were riding and where they had boarded, and risk the fragile stillness of the car breaking open. Or she could take a seat at the next table over, order nothing, and listen, letting the dining-car regulars reveal themselves in their own time, the way a photograph develops in a darkroom.

{~HERO:Vera~} pulled out a chair and sat. The man in the coat looked at her then, and his eyes were a pale watery blue that seemed to have been looking at her for a very long time before she sat down. “You’re new,” he said, and it wasn’t a question. The woman with the gloves said nothing, but she turned her cup in small precise circles on the saucer, and {~HERO:Vera~} saw that the cup was empty—had been empty the whole time—and the steam rising from it was coming from the cup itself, the porcelain faintly warm, as though something had been poured into it a long time ago and never drunk. The fact landed like a stone: these passengers weren’t waiting for the dining car to open. They were waiting for a meal that had already been served, on a night that had already passed, and they had been waiting so long that waiting had become the meal.

{~HERO:Vera~} took a seat two tables away and watched the dining-car regulars in the window glass, their reflections laid over the dark country like a double exposure. After a while the man in the coat spoke, not to her but to the table, a low murmur she had to strain to hear. “They change the timetable every season,” he said, “but the north line never does.” The woman with the gloves nodded without lifting her head. The observation was small, almost too small to hold, but it rang against something {~HERO:Vera~} had already begun to feel: the train was not on a schedule. It was on a loop, a season the line kept for itself, and these passengers had been riding it for years. She could hold the thread and follow it forward, or she could let the warmth of the carriage pull her under and lose the shape of what she had almost heard.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The dining-car regulars had given {~HERO:Vera~} the same truth from two angles: they were not passengers in the ordinary sense. They were fixtures. The train carried them the way a house carries its furniture, and the empty cups and the steam without smell and the man’s quiet remark about the north line were all pieces of a larger stillness. The journey drew tight around her. The carriage swayed, and the lamps flickered once, and in the flicker {~HERO:Vera~} felt the whole long weight of the night press against her, a held breath waiting for release.

The dining car had told {~HERO:Vera~} something she couldn’t unhear: the train was carrying more than travellers. It was carrying a whole season, a stretch of time that had been lifted out of the calendar and laid along these rails, and the passengers were its keepers. She walked forward through the swaying cars and the question that had been pulling at her since the platform was sharper now, a hook set in her chest, drawing her toward the tunnel and whatever waited on the other side of the dark.

Before she left the dining car, {~HERO:Vera~} caught one more detail from the regulars at the table by the window. The woman with the gloves had turned her cup over, and on the underside of the saucer there was a date stamped in blue ink—a year, nothing more. The year was twenty-seven years ago. {~HERO:Vera~} filed the fact away without knowing what it meant, and when she walked forward into the next carriage she was carrying it like a small cold key. It did not unlock the whole train, not yet, but it was real and it was hers, a hard bright piece of the night she could keep.

The child was sitting alone in the last row of the third carriage, legs too short to reach the floor, eyes open and calm and fixed on the aisle as though she had been waiting for {~HERO:Vera~} to walk through the door. She was perhaps eight, perhaps older—there was something in the stillness of her face that made age hard to read. The carriage swayed and the cold glass threw {~HERO:Vera~}’s reflection over the dark, a woman approaching a child who did not blink. The child wore a red coat and held nothing in her hands, and the seat beside her was empty, and the whole carriage seemed to have arranged itself around her the way a room arranges itself around a lit candle. A detail pricked at {~HERO:Vera~}’s attention: the child’s breath did not fog the window beside her.

The child watched {~HERO:Vera~} approach with the patient, unsurprised attention of someone who had seen many passengers walk this aisle and knew which ones would stop. Her hands lay open on her lap, and her red coat was buttoned to the throat, and the carriage around her was warmer than the rest of the train, a pocket of heat that had no obvious source. Two ways to meet her opened. {~HERO:Vera~} could sit down in the empty seat beside the child and ask her directly who she was and why she was awake, risking whatever answer might come from a mouth that looked so young and eyes that looked so old. Or she could take the seat across the aisle and wait, letting the child decide whether to speak, and whether to tell the truth.

{~HERO:Vera~} sat down beside the child, and the seat was warm as though someone had just risen from it. “What’s your name?” {~HERO:Vera~} asked, and the child turned her head slowly, the way a very old person turns their head, careful of the neck. “I don’t have one anymore,” the child said. “I gave it to the conductor when I got on.” The words were delivered flatly, without self-pity, a simple statement of fact. The fact settled into {~HERO:Vera~}’s mind and would not move: the child had been on the train so long that she had traded her name for passage, and the conductor’s clock was keeping it.

{~HERO:Vera~} took the seat across the aisle and let the child decide. For a long time the child said nothing, only watched the aisle with her calm unblinking eyes, and then she spoke without turning her head. “You’re wondering why I’m awake.” Her voice was small but clear, a voice that had been speaking to strangers on trains for a very long time. “I’m awake because someone has to be. The tunnel is close, and not everyone on this train is going to make it through.” The observation landed like a cold hand on the back of {~HERO:Vera~}’s neck. She could hold the thread and follow it forward into whatever the child knew, or she could let the hour and the warmth of the carriage pull her under and wake with nothing but the memory of a warning she hadn’t heeded.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The child in the red coat had given {~HERO:Vera~} a truth that bent the air around it. Whether she had spoken of names or of tunnels, the weight was the same: the train was carrying passengers who were not quite passengers, who had traded something essential for their place aboard, and the tunnel ahead was a threshold that not all of them would cross. The carriage seemed to contract around the knowledge, the walls drawing in, the lamps dimming a fraction. Even the wheels on the iron had gone quieter, as though the train itself were listening.

The child had given {~HERO:Vera~} a question she couldn’t let go of: what did it cost to ride this train, and who had paid? She walked forward through the swaying cars and the question walked with her, a small cold companion, and the whole train seemed to be breathing around it. The lamps flickered, and the couplings gave their low iron sigh, and {~HERO:Vera~} moved toward the centre of the night the way a moth moves toward a window.

Before she left the carriage, {~HERO:Vera~} knelt down and tucked the edge of the child’s red coat under her leg so it wouldn’t drag on the floor. The child looked at her then, really looked, and in her eyes there was something so old and so tired that {~HERO:Vera~}’s breath caught. “Thank you,” the child said, and the two words were the warmest thing {~HERO:Vera~} had heard all night. The exchange was small—a coat, a thank-you—but it was real and it was hers, a moment of ordinary kindness on a train that was anything but ordinary. She carried it forward like a small lit thing, not enough to light the whole night, but enough to see by.

The man was sitting three rows from the back, leaning toward the window with his lips moving, a low murmur that {~HERO:Vera~} couldn’t quite make out over the sound of the wheels. The carriage swayed, and the cold glass threw back her reflection, a woman pausing in the aisle, and behind her reflection the dark country was still unreeling with its impossible lit stations and its single patient figure. The man counted softly, rhythmically, the way a rosary is counted, and every few breaths he would pause and shake his head and start again from a lower number. A detail caught at {~HERO:Vera~}: his eyes were closed, and he was counting stations that the train had not yet passed.

The man wore a dark coat and his hands were folded on his lap, the fingers moving slightly as he counted, a ceaseless small motion like a heartbeat. {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the aisle and the man did not open his eyes, did not acknowledge her, and yet the rhythm of his counting seemed to shift when she stopped, as though he were counting her presence among the stations. Two ways to approach him opened. She could sit down beside him, touch his sleeve, ask him what he was counting and why the numbers never ended, and risk pulling him out of whatever deep water he was swimming in. Or she could take the seat behind him and listen, letting the soft stream of numbers tell her their own story, the stations that never came and the terminus that was always one hour off.

{~HERO:Vera~} sat down beside the man and touched his sleeve. His eyes opened at once, pale and unsurprised, and the counting stopped. “You’re the one who found the letter,” he said, and it wasn’t a question. “I’ve been counting the stations since I got on, and there are always more of them than there were the night before. The line is growing.” He turned back to the window, and the counting resumed, but not from where he had left off—from a number {~HERO:Vera~} hadn’t heard him reach. The fact settled into her like a splinter: the north line wasn’t a route. It was a living thing, and it was getting longer.

{~HERO:Vera~} took the seat behind the man and closed her eyes, letting his soft counting wash over her. The numbers were irregular—not a true count but a kind of music, rising and falling, pausing at stations that had names she couldn’t quite hear. After a while she noticed that the man was counting backwards, or seemed to be, the numbers growing smaller instead of larger, and she understood that he wasn’t counting the stations ahead. He was counting the stations behind, the ones the train had already passed, and he was losing track of them. The observation was fragile, a soap bubble of a thought, but it carried a weight: the train was not only travelling north. It was erasing its own path. She could hold the thread and follow it forward, or she could let the hour and the motion pull her under before she had to decide what it meant.

nodes.body: The signal lamps were burning ahead of the tunnel mouth, two red lights and a green one, hanging in the dark above the snow like low stars. {~HERO:Vera~} stood at the forward window of the fifth carriage and watched them, and the carriage swayed, and the cold glass held her reflection over the dark, a woman peering into a night that was growing deeper and stranger by the mile. The lamps were railway lamps, standard issue, but they were burning with a light that seemed to have no source—no oil, no electricity, a pure cold flame that didn’t flicker in the wind. A detail caught at her: the green lamp was the one that should have been red, and it was burning steadily, and the train was still moving toward the tunnel.

The tunnel mouth was growing in the forward windows, a black arch carved into the mountain, and the signal lamps above it were steady and silent. {~HERO:Vera~} pressed her forehead to the cold glass and watched the lamps, trying to read what they were saying. Two ways to interpret them opened. She could trust that the green meant what green always meant—proceed, go forward, the tunnel was clear—and let the train carry her into the dark without questioning the signal. Or she could study the lamps more carefully, watch for a flicker, a shift, the moment when the wrong-coloured light might change, and in doing so risk learning something about the tunnel that she wasn’t ready to know.

{~HERO:Vera~} kept her eyes on the green lamp and waited. Just before the train reached the tunnel mouth, the green light blinked—once, deliberately, the way a person blinks—and in the instant of darkness that followed she saw something she had not seen before. The lamps were not mounted on posts. They were mounted on the tunnel itself, driven into the rock, and the rock was not rock. It was a face. A huge stone face, weathered and patient, and the tunnel mouth was its open mouth. The fact was a cold shock: the mountain was not a mountain. It was a threshold carved into the shape of something that had been waiting, and the green light was an invitation.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed at the window and watched the lamps without pressing. After a while she noticed that the green lamp was not the only one burning wrong. The two red lamps were burning too, but they were not red—they were a deep amber, the colour of old honey, and they were pulsing faintly, a slow rhythm that matched the sway of the carriage. The observation was soft, almost too soft to hold, but it carried a weight: the signals were not railway signals. They were part of the train, part of the night, part of the season the train was carrying, and they were speaking a language {~HERO:Vera~} could almost understand. The green light was not “proceed.” It was “come.” She could hold the thread and follow it forward, or she could let the cold and the dark pull her under before the choice came.

ending.title: No One Will Meet Your Eye

nodes.body: The train had slowed to a walking pace, and the conductor was standing in the vestibule at the very front of the fifth carriage, his silver punch-clock held loosely at his side, his pale eyes on the black arch of the tunnel that filled the forward windows. {~HERO:Vera~} walked toward him and the carriage swayed, the cold glass holding her reflection over the dark, a woman approaching a man who had been waiting for her since the platform. The air was sharp with cold and the smell of wet rock, and the conductor’s breath came in long slow plumes. This time he turned before she reached him. “You’re ready,” he said, and it wasn’t a question. A detail caught at her: his punch-clock was open, the card half-drawn, and the names on it were glowing faintly in the dark.

The conductor held the clock between them, and the card inside was dense with names, dozens of them, hundreds, written in a dozen different hands. Some were fresh, the ink still wet. Some were so old they were nearly invisible, faded to a pale silver shimmer that was only visible when the clock was tilted toward the light. {~HERO:Vera~} stood in the narrow vestibule with the tunnel mouth growing in the window behind the conductor’s head, and two ways to meet him opened. She could ask him to explain the north line—all of it, the names, the stations, the tunnel, the dawn—and risk the fragile quiet of the moment breaking before she had her answer. Or she could let him speak in his own time, trusting that the conductor who had carried the clock since before she was born would tell her what she needed to know, and no more.

“Tell me,” {~HERO:Vera~} said, and the conductor looked at her for a long moment with his pale unblinking eyes. “The north line isn’t a railway,” he said. “It’s a passage. Every season the train runs once, from the platform to the tunnel, and every passenger aboard is someone who needs to let go of something before the dawn. The clock keeps the names of the ones who aren’t ready. When the tunnel opens, the names go back to their owners, and the owners step down onto the other side.” The fact settled into {~HERO:Vera~}’s chest like a stone: the train was a ferry, and the river was the night, and the far shore was the first grey dawn.

{~HERO:Vera~} said nothing, and after a moment the conductor spoke anyway, his voice softer now, the voice of a man who had been saying the same words for a very long time. “Every passenger on this train is riding toward the tunnel,” he said, “but not every passenger will go through. Some will ride on into the next season, and the next, until they’re ready to set down what they’re carrying. The tunnel doesn’t judge. It waits.” He touched the clock, and the names on the card dimmed. The observation was soft, not hard enough to hold, but it carried a weight: the conductor was not the keeper of the clock. He was one of the names on it, and he had been waiting longer than anyone. She could hold the thread and follow it forward, or she could let the cold and the dark pull her under before the choice came.
